label: Group Actions and Quasi-Isometries
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 131 to 152 and turns a finitely generated group into a geometric object. We fix the word metric, draw the Cayley graph, and ask which features survive when distance is only known up to a linear distortion. That coarse viewpoint is the whole game.

label: Actions by Isometries
notes: A group acts by isometries when every element moves points without changing distances. Stress the orbit and stabilizer language, and that the action descends to a metric on the quotient only under good hypotheses. Free, isometric actions are the bridge between algebra and the metric geometry that follows.

label: Proper and Cocompact Actions
notes: Properness controls how the group sits discretely inside the isometries; cocompactness says a compact piece tiles the whole space under the action. Together they make the action geometric. Emphasise that these two finiteness conditions are exactly what the Svarc-Milnor lemma will consume as hypotheses.

label: The Word Metric
notes: Pick a finite generating set, write each element as a shortest word, and the word length becomes a left-invariant metric on the group. Different generating sets change the numbers but not the coarse shape. Make clear that the metric depends on a choice yet its large-scale geometry does not.

label: The Cayley Graph
notes: The Cayley graph realises the group as the vertex set of a connected graph with generator edges. Path distance in this graph is exactly the word metric. Show the square grid for the free abelian group of rank two so students see algebra become a concrete metric graph they can walk along.

label: Quasi-Isometries
notes: A quasi-isometry allows multiplicative stretching by L and additive slack by C, plus a coarse surjectivity condition. It is the right notion of sameness for large-scale geometry because it forgets bounded detail. Walk through why the relation is symmetric up to constants and genuinely an equivalence on spaces.

label: Quasi-Geodesics
notes: A quasi-geodesic is the image of an interval under a quasi-isometric embedding, so it travels efficiently up to fixed constants. These paths are the working tool of coarse geometry. Mention that in hyperbolic spaces quasi-geodesics stay uniformly close to honest geodesics, a stability fact we will need later.

label: The Svarc-Milnor Lemma
notes: State the lemma carefully: a group acting geometrically on a length space is finitely generated and quasi-isometric to that space, via the orbit map. This is the fundamental theorem of geometric group theory. Underline that it converts a metric action into an intrinsic statement about the group itself.

label: The Orbit Map
notes: Fix a basepoint and send each group element to its image under the action. The Svarc-Milnor hypotheses make this orbit map a quasi-isometry. Use the picture of the integer lattice orbit inside the plane to show generators becoming unit translations and word length tracking Euclidean distance up to constants.

label: Z-squared and the Plane
notes: The free abelian group of rank two acts on the Euclidean plane by integer translations, geometrically. So its Cayley grid is quasi-isometric to the plane. The taxicab word metric and the Euclidean metric differ by a bounded factor, the cleanest worked instance of the whole machinery in action.

label: Quasi-Isometry Invariants
notes: Properties preserved by quasi-isometry are the legitimate invariants: growth type, number of ends, and Gromov hyperbolicity among them. Because of Svarc-Milnor these become invariants of the group up to commensurability. Frame invariants as the payoff: they let coarse geometry distinguish groups that algebra alone struggles to separate.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the pipeline: isometric geometric action, word metric, Cayley graph, quasi-isometry, Svarc-Milnor, invariants. The reader should leave able to compute a word metric, sketch a Cayley graph, and name what survives coarsening. Next chapters apply this to non-positively curved spaces and their boundaries.
